 USDA: SNAP fraud costs NY $1 billion without including Trump policy bill
 BY 
 David Jacobs
 Syracuse 
 PUBLISHED 10:29 AM ET Oct. 22, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 10:29 AM EDT Oct. 22, 2026 
 SHARE 
 Many states like New York are reportedly going to be fined $1 billion in 2028 unless they cooperate with the federal government's efforts to curb what it terms electronic benefits transfer fraud in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
 U.S. Department of Agriculture Deputy Secretary Stephen Vaden said he fears the $1 billion tax may be dispersed throughout individual counties across the state and not necessarily be taken care of by the state government.
 "New York will be penalized by federal law because it has failed to clean up its rolls and ensure that the money taxpayers provide for the most needy only goes to the most needy," he said.
 New York's payment error rates, according to USDA reports, are over 10%, as is the national average.
 "If you're receiving benefits from each of those states and the taxpayer twice over," Vaden said, "we don't know it because those governors don't want to cooperate with this effort."
 Onondaga County Executive Ryan McMahon said any government program like SNAP is going to be abused, or people will find loopholes — which could include stealing benefits of qualified people after their deaths.
 Roughly 151,000 deceased people have been deleted off benefits, Vaden said, as the Social Security Administration gives up-to-date data about its benefit-holders.
 In Onondaga County, just approximately 4.5% of a few thousand SNAP fraud investigations conducted resulted in proven fraud, a county official said, and the value of all local cases in 2025 was a little more than $600,000.
 Vaden believes finding fraudulent transactions "costs the states and counties nothing," saying the USDA conducted more than 170 undercover investigations in New York state.
 The New York State Association of Counties showed many counties are already under fiscal stress, as counties outside of New York City are already seeing $58 million in additional costs as a result of the Trump policy bill which went into effect Oct. 1. 
 Local increases in costs project to be around a 4% increase in Erie County and a 3% increase in Monroe County, and those costs are before the penalty payments to the state are doled out.
 The federal share of SNAP administrative funding was dropped from 50% to 25% in the Trump policy bill.
 Gov. Kathy Hochul's office did not respond to a request for comment.
 The state is moving forward with more secure, chip-enabled EBT cards in 2027.
